extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, classics, and ancient political/philosophical thought
extracted.subtask_description: Close literary and philosophical commentary on Books III–IV of Plato's Republic, extracting evaluative principles about education, art, legislation, and character formation. Aimed at analyzing Plato's prescriptions and stylistic methods rather than producing a new work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style should conform to subject; metre to style
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match linguistic register and formal features (e.g., metre) to the nature of the subject-matter; avoid disproportion between thought and expression. Example/anti-pattern: letting elaborate rhetoric outrun or obscure the thought, or using obscure phrasing where clarity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of simplicity and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The simplicity and harmony of the soul should be reflected in [style and metre].’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple, harmonious expression and forms across arts; complexity that corrupts taste should be avoided. The author treats simplicity as something to be learned early and drawn from nature and crafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists must avoid meanness or unseemliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture, painting, and music must conform to the law of simplicity; those who violate it 'cannot be allowed to work' and corrupt citizens' taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that presents deformity or unseemly forms is morally and educationally dangerous for youth and guardianship cultures; censor or exclude such works from civic upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical education shapes the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Of all these influences the greatest is the education given by music, which finds a way into the innermost soul and imparts to it the sense of beauty and of deformity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use music as a core formative element in education; choose musical forms that inculcate moral harmony. Beware that music's early effects are unconscious but durable when reason matures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic education must fit guardian temper
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastics should be tailored to guardians: warrior athletes require a simpler kind of gymnastic akin to their simple music, be 'wide-awake', and inured to changes of food and climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design physical training to produce alert, hardy defenders (not sleepy general gymnastic routines). Avoid sudden cessation of unsuitable training that endangers health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary simplicity for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Dietary rule modelled on Homer: heroes fed on roast meat only; avoid fish, boiled meats, sweet sauces and elaborate cookery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote simple, robust diets for guardians to prevent luxury and intemperance. Anti-patterns include elaborate cuisines and indulgent practices (Sicilian/Attic confections, courtesans) which corrupt social health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutional expansion caused by luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Where gluttony and intemperance prevail the town fills with doctors and pleaders; law and medicine gain airs when freemen indulge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/education should reduce the causes of frivolous litigation and medicalization by discouraging luxury and self-indulgence. Implicit evaluation: societies that foster dependency on legal or medical services indicate moral decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician should have personal experience of illness; judge should not have experience of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The physician should have had experience of disease in his own body... the judge controls mind by mind; and therefore his mind should not be corrupted by crime.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign professional suitability differently: medical practitioners benefit from intimate knowledge of suffering; judicial officers should be morally uncorrupted and gain insight into vice by observation, not practice. Use age and moral history as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges should be mature and morally formed
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge should be of a certain age; his youth should have been innocent and he should acquire insight into evil later by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require tests of maturity and prior innocence for judicial office to prevent corruption or suspect temperament. Caution against appointing overly young judges lacking moral discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance music and gymnastic to harmonize soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Music tames and gymnastic arouses and sustains the soul; too much of either produces imbalance (enervation or brutalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational programs must mix intellectual/musical and physical training to cultivate reason and spiritedness in harmony. Anti-patterns: overemphasis on music leading to lack of spirit, or overemphasis on athletics producing brute force without counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler selection: love of subjects and tested character
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers should be elders who love their subjects, see a common interest with them, and have been tried by many tests to ensure they retain opinions and resist force, enchantment, pleasure, and grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select leaders for demonstrated disinterestedness and steadfastness under diverse trials (danger, pleasure, grief). Use repeated trials across life-epochs to check stability of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foundational myth ('magnificent lie') to secure civic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell a graduated legend (first rulers, then soldiers, then people) that citizens were fashioned in the earth and descended from different metals to bind them to the State and to teach duty; present as a verisimilar myth rather than literal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ civic myth-making strategically to inculcate solidarity and duty. Sequence and audience matter: impart first to rulers, then soldiers, then populace. The myth frees discussion of social transposition and justifies institutions pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must have no private property or household wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should have no property, common meals, pay only meeting expenses, may not touch gold or silver or be under the same roof with it; private land/household turns them into householders and tyrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement economic restrictions on guardians to prevent conflicts of interest and luxury; prohibit accumulation or contact with private wealth. Anti-pattern: guardians owning property becomes a path to tyranny and social ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of ranks: meritocratic mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Plato posits natural ranks, he insists these distinctions should be broken through by personal qualities; movement up or down the social scale must be possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create systems of selection and testing that allow talented individuals to rise regardless of birth; periodically override inherited caste to preserve rule by the best.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art: simple, ideal, morally expressive
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘True art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple and ideal,—the expression of the highest moral energy, whether in action or repose.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge art by its capacity to express and inculcate moral energy and ideal forms rather than mere imitation or fanciful obscurity. Promote exposure to such works in youth to form taste. Anti-pattern: art that is merely imitative or indulgent in novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic style demands clarity, proportion, and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should avoid obscurity; there must be proportion between style and subject, ease and clearness, and 'music adding the expression of feeling to thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetic passages for clarity and appropriate diction; watch for half-expressed figures, harsh constructions, distorted collocations, or remote idea sequences. The ideal is balance akin to a 'Greek statue'—nothing to add or take away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical techniques to sustain reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato employs affected ignorance of music, tentative construction, oscillation between reality and imagination, connecting links toward larger moves (e.g., expulsion of poets), and companion pictures and satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical devices like feigned modesty, tentative exposition, alternating modes (imagined vs. real) and illustrative contrasts to maintain engagement and to introduce controversial proposals gently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve core cultural forms: preserve songs and training from innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The governors' care should preserve music and gymnastic from innovation; changing songs leads to altering laws and ultimately social ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat certain cultural forms (songs, training regimens) as stabilizing institutions; avoid frivolous or radical innovations which may have cascading moral and political consequences. Anticipate slow, secret erosion from seemingly innocent changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic middle condition is best for citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A middle condition is best for artisans; they should have money enough to buy tools, and not enough to be independent of business.’ This middle condition is recommended also for citizens to avoid meanness or luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design economic policy to support moderate means for classes—enough for instruments and tools but not wealth that generates luxury or dependence. Evaluate social arrangements by their tendency to produce either meanness (poverty) or laziness/luxury (riches).

rubrics_metrics.name: State size constrained by unity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To the size of the state there is no limit but the necessity of unity; it must be neither too large nor too small to be one.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess optimal polity size by capacity to maintain unity of purpose and cohesion; avoid scales that undermine the notion of a single common state. This is a secondary design criterion compared with education and unity of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of education: state exists for duty not private happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is 'the great matter' and without it a state cannot progress; the constitution is designed for the good of the whole, not to make citizens happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize comprehensive education (musical, gymnastic, moral) as the central instrument of statecraft. Evaluate policies by whether they support formative education that secures public good over private indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use myth and poetic appeal rather than strict logical argument for social lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth is 'more interesting' and enables imparting new principles lightly; Plato adapts Homeric and mythic material rhetorically to instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching civic principles, consider narrative/moral exempla to engage audiences and circumvent resistance; recognize limits of strict logic in persuading broader publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style notes — list of lesser stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of stylistic remarks: (1) affected ignorance of music, (2) tentative manner, (3) alternating description as reality and imagination, (4) connecting links toward poet expulsion, (5) companion pictures and satirical jests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing similar philosophical dialogue, attend to these devices as tools to shape tone and argument progression; they are small but significant elements that sustain interest and rhetorical force.
